title: REST API Design with Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Building REST APIs is the most common task for backend Go engineers, and interviewers probe this module to verify you have opinions beyond just spinning up a Chi or Gin router. They want to see that you understand versioning tradeoffs, can explain why cursor-based pagination scales better than offset, know how to issue and validate JWTs without relying on middleware magic boxes, understand the token-bucket model underlying most rate limiters, and can instrument a graceful shutdown so in-flight requests complete cleanly during a rolling deploy. These are the day-to-day engineering decisions that separate a competent API developer from a junior one.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: A Go REST API is built around an http.Handler chain: a router (net/http ServeMux, Chi, or Gin) dispatches requests to handlers, and middleware wraps each handler to inject cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, rate limiting, tracing). Middleware in Go is just a function that takes an http.Handler and returns an http.Handler — no framework magic required. JWT authentication is stateless: the client sends a signed token, the server verifies the signature and expiry locally without a database round-trip. Graceful shutdown uses http.Server.Shutdown(ctx) which stops accepting new connections, then waits for active connections to drain before the process exits. OpenAPI (via swaggo) is generated from Go struct annotations and serves a Swagger UI endpoint for API exploration.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. API versioning — URL path (/v1/), Accept header, or subdomain; path versioning is most common and most tool-friendly. 2. Cursor-based pagination — encode the last-seen ID or timestamp as an opaque cursor; avoids the OFFSET drift problem as rows are inserted/deleted. 3. JWT structure — header.payload.signature; verify with the correct algorithm (RS256 or HS256), check exp, iss, aud claims; never trust the alg field from the token header. 4. Rate limiting middleware — token bucket (golang.org/x/time/rate) per IP or per user; return 429 with Retry-After header. 5. swaggo/swag — go generate runs swag init, produces docs/swagger.json, served via swaggerFiles handler. 6. Graceful shutdown — listen for SIGTERM/SIGINT, call server.Shutdown(ctx) with a deadline, wait for the server goroutine to exit. 7. Middleware chain — log request ID, recover from panics, enforce auth, check rate limit — order matters. 8. Error response shape — consistent JSON envelope {error: {code, message}} helps clients parse errors reliably.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: Why is cursor-based pagination better than LIMIT/OFFSET for large tables? — OFFSET causes the database to scan and discard N rows on every page; with insertions the page windows shift, causing duplicate or skipped rows. Cursor-based uses a WHERE id > cursor LIMIT n which hits an index directly. Q: How do you prevent the alg:none JWT attack? — Always specify the allowed algorithm explicitly in your verification function (jwt.ParseWithClaims with a key function that only accepts RS256/HS256); never trust the alg from the token header. Q: What is the token bucket algorithm and how does golang.org/x/time/rate implement it? — Tokens accumulate at a fixed rate up to a burst cap; each request consumes one token; Allow() returns false when the bucket is empty. rate.NewLimiter(r, b) sets rate r and burst b. Q: How does http.Server.Shutdown differ from http.Server.Close? — Shutdown gracefully waits for active connections to finish; Close immediately terminates all connections. Q: What is the correct signal handling pattern for graceful shutdown in Go? — Signal.Notify into a channel, receive the signal in a goroutine, then call server.Shutdown with a context deadline.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "For REST API versioning I default to URL path versioning — /v1/, /v2/ — because it's explicit, easy to test in a browser, and plays nicely with API gateways and documentation tools. For pagination on any endpoint that could return more than a few hundred rows I use cursor-based pagination: the response includes a next_cursor field which encodes the last item's ID or created_at; the next request passes it as a query param and we do WHERE id > cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT n, which always hits the primary key index. For auth I validate JWTs locally with a fixed algorithm allowlist — I never trust the alg field in the token itself. Graceful shutdown is wired at startup: I listen for SIGTERM, call server.Shutdown with a 30-second context, and block until it returns — that way rolling deploys complete in-flight requests cleanly."
